proof:
The shear preserves symmetry, masses and anchored inclusions. Work in the sheared coordinates, put $m=d+1$ and $\Gamma=(d/m)^d$, and write $K=K_p$ and $V=|K|$. With $a^*=m^{-1}\mathbf1$, use the cap groups
$$
H_i(a)=\{l_i(x)-(a_i-1/m)(v\cdot z)\ge0\},\qquad \sum_i a_i=1.
$$
Their margins sum to zero, and at $p$ the $i$th restriction is $\lambda_i(x)\ge a_i$. Each cap is nonvertical and through the origin, so symmetry gives the common original mass $M/2$ for every such $a$.

Apply finite-base-ball-strictification-and-symmetric-cap-flatness after the shear, with $\phi_z=R-|z|^2$ for $R>\max_z|z|^2$. Use the unnormalized rounded fibers $\widehat K_z^\varepsilon=K_z+\varepsilon\phi_z B_d$ with total $\widehat M_\varepsilon$. Every excluded-self support gap is at least $\varepsilon\Delta_P^2$ and the product Hausdorff neighborhood of radius $\varepsilon\Delta_P^2/4$ is actually compatible. The unchanged rounded family is symmetric and all its caps $H_i(a)$ have mass $\widehat M_\varepsilon/2$. Fix the other fibers and change the selected one to $Q(W)+\tau B_d$, where $\tau=\varepsilon\phi_p$ and the columns of $W$ are its underlying simplex's labeled barycentric vertices near $I$, with column sums one. Let $V_\varepsilon(W)$ be the change of selected-fiber volume and let $F_{\varepsilon i}(W,a)$ be its cap volume in $\{\lambda_i\ge a_i\}$. The exact global cap increment from $\widehat M_\varepsilon/2$ is
$$
C_{\varepsilon i}(W,a)=F_{\varepsilon i}(W,a)-F_{\varepsilon i}(I,a).
$$
This uses only reflection of the unchanged family and cancels every unchanged fiber contribution without differentiating it. The rounded-simplex-cap-face-tube-polynomial lemma applies since near $(I,a^*)$ precisely vertex $i$ has positive margin in each selected restriction, uniformly on a smaller neighborhood. Thus $V_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon$ extend smoothly to $\varepsilon=0$ with all derivatives through order two converging there.

At zero rounding the normalized $i$th cap formula is
$$
P_i(W,a)=F_{0i}(W,a)/V=\det W\,\frac{(W_{ii}-a_i)^d}{\prod_{j\ne i}(W_{ii}-W_{ij})}.
$$
It follows from the edge ratios of the one-vertex cap, with the volume determinant as in e42e4ad8eaa4f705. The fixed-$a^*$ first derivative is $f_i(B)=\Gamma[\operatorname{tr}B+(B\mathbf1)_i]$ for zero-column-sum $B$. Its right inverse is the map $S$ given by $z_i=y_i/(m\Gamma)$, $Z=\sum_i z_i$, $S(y)_{ii}=z_i$, $S(y)_{ij}=z_i-Z/d$ for $i\ne j$. Indeed the columns sum to zero, the trace is $Z$, and the $i$th row sum is $mz_i-Z$. Hence the right inverse for absolute cap derivatives is $\mathcal R y=S(y/V)$. The physical objective derivative is $V\operatorname{tr}B=(m\Gamma)^{-1}\sum_i V f_i(B)$, and all pure threshold derivatives of $C_0(I,a)$ vanish.

Here is the positive joint curvature, including the needed mixed block. Take the matrix $E$ with $E_{01}=1,E_{11}=-1$ and other entries zero, and set $B_0=E-S(f(E))$, $\omega=e_1-e_0$. Then $f(B_0)=0$, $\operatorname{tr}B_0=0$, and $B_0\mathbf1=0$. Its diagonal $b$ has entries $b_0=0,b_1=-(d-1)/m,b_i=1/m$ for $i\ge2$. Its off-diagonal entries are $(d-1)/d$ at $(0,1)$, $-1/d$ at $(0,j)$ for $j\ge2$, $(d-1)/(md)$ in row $1$ off the diagonal, and $-1/(md)$ in every other off-diagonal entry. Consequently $\|b\|^2=d(d-1)/m^2$ and $\|B_0-\operatorname{diag} b\|_F^2=(d-1)/d+(d-1)/m^2$. The fixed-threshold Hessian of
$$
L=V_0-(m\Gamma)^{-1}\sum_i C_{0i}
$$
divided by $V$ is $\|b\|^2/(dm)-\|B_0-\operatorname{diag}b\|_F^2/m=-(d-1)/(dm)$ by e42e4ad8eaa4f705, since the row and column sums of the off-diagonal part are both $-b$. The mixed derivative of $P_i$ is $\Gamma (m^2/d)b_i\omega_i$: differentiating its physical log derivative in $a_i$ gives $d b_i/(1-a_i)^2$, while the derivative of the prefactor multiplies the zero physical first derivative. Thus the mixed block of $L/V$ is $-(m/d)b\cdot\omega=(d-1)/d$. Its pure threshold block vanishes because $C_0(I,a)$ vanishes identically. The full first derivative of $L$ is zero, and its joint Hessian on $(B_0,\omega)$ is $VQ$ where $Q=(d-1)(2-1/m)/d>0$.

Set $W(t,r)=I+tB_0+\mathcal R r$ and $a(t)=a^*+t\omega$. The $r$ derivative of $C_0(W(t,r),a(t))$ at zero is the identity, so the implicit function theorem gives a smooth correction $r(t,\varepsilon)$ solving $C_\varepsilon=0$ with $r(0,\varepsilon)=0$. At zero rounding $r_t(0,0)=0$. The reduced gain $J_\varepsilon(t)=V_\varepsilon(W(t,r(t,\varepsilon)))$ satisfies $J_\varepsilon(0)=0$. At zero rounding it is also the value of $L$ along this curve, since all the cap increments vanish. The first derivative of $L$ is zero and the curve has tangent $(B_0,\omega)$, so $J_0''(0)=VQ$. Smoothness makes $J_\varepsilon''(0)>0$ for all sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$. For each such fixed $\varepsilon$, the symmetric difference $J_\varepsilon(t)+J_\varepsilon(-t)-2J_\varepsilon(0)$ is positive for all sufficiently small $t>0$. One sign gives positive volume gain with all cap increments still zero. The chosen $t$ can be arbitrarily small, so the moving fiber stays inside the actual compatibility neighborhood. At that point the $r$ Jacobian is still invertible. Changing the target of the implicit equation to $-\eta\mathbf1$ for a sufficiently small $\eta>0$ strictly decreases every cap mass and retains the strict volume gain and open compatibility. The cap group still covers the whole ambient space.

Finally apply the common dilation $\alpha_\varepsilon=(M/\widehat M_\varepsilon)^{1/d}$ to the fibers and their cap planes. It restores the baseline total and budgets to $M$ and $M/2$ and preserves both strict inequalities. The cap margins become $l_i(x)-\alpha_\varepsilon(a_i-1/m)(v\cdot z)$ and still sum to zero. Since $\alpha_\varepsilon\to1$, choosing $\varepsilon$ and then the selected-fiber change and negative budget target sufficiently small gives the claimed neighborhood result.

For a larger compact original body, its positive integer bases are lattice-complete: each integer convex combination of positive fibers contains a Minkowski combination with positive volume. Their hull preserves the measured fibers. In deficient base rank, the saturated lattice in $\operatorname{span}P$ extends to an ambient lattice basis, so apply the proof in the occupied coordinates. A product with a centered transverse cube of side less than one contributes no transverse nonzero integer base and hence preserves all integer fibers and the extended cap budgets. These operations concern the retained finite geometry.

For the initially active triangle model of the source, the midpoint body $(K-K)/2$ has area $3/4$ and perimeter $2+\sqrt2$: it is the hexagon with vertices one half the cyclic difference vectors of the standard coordinate triangle. The endpoint triangles have area $1/2$ each and the same perimeter. Radii $(\varepsilon,2\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ add exactly $\varepsilon B$ of midpoint slack and give unnormalized total area $7/4+4(2+\sqrt2)\varepsilon+6\pi\varepsilon^2$ by the planar tube formula. The zero-rounding reduced Hessian in this example is $(1/2)(5/6)=5/12$.

statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $d\ge2$, and let $P=\operatorname{conv}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^n$ be finite, centrally symmetric about $0$, and affinely spanning. Let positive compact convex fibers $K_z\subset\mathbb R^d$ satisfy all anchored Minkowski inclusions and $K_{-z}=-K_z$. Suppose $K_p$ is a simplex at a nonzero $p\in P$. Fix a linear functional $v$ with $v\cdot p=1$ and apply the fiber-preserving shear $(z,x)\mapsto(z,x-c(v\cdot z))$ for the centroid $c$ of $K_p$. In these coordinates write the selected simplex barycentric functions as $\lambda_i=l_i+1/(d+1)$. Let $M=\sum_z|K_z|$.

In every neighborhood of the original fibers in product Hausdorff distance and their canonical cap group $\{l_i(x)\ge0\}_{i=0}^d$ in plane parameters, there is a compatible family on the same positive integer bases and a nearby group of $d+1$ closed caps covering the whole ambient space, with new total mass $>M$ and each new selected cap mass $<M/2$. The perturbed fibers are realized by their actual lifted convex hull. If only the positive-fiber hull of a larger body is considered, this is a neighborhood statement for the retained geometry. A deficient base span can be handled in its intrinsic lattice, with an optional full-dimensional ambient completion preserving all integer fibers and these cap masses.
title: Cap-flat symmetric rounding allows simultaneous selected-cap descent
